“The books in which he had written down material from the eloquent Arabs filled one of his rooms almost to the ceiling.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
All these historical examples show clearly that the movement toward written recording developed alongside the rise of cultural activity and the emergence of the Arab sciences.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
It also developed alongside the intellectual movement that had begun, in its earliest stage, as a reflection of the intense political conflict of the early Umayyad period.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
It was therefore natural for writing to become another force helping cultural exchange between the Arabs and the peoples of the vast Arab state.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
This exchange would later bear fruit in the development of Arab-Islamic thought.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Written transmission also played an important part in spreading the rational thought of the Muʿtazila, which was becoming increasingly active within these same political and cultural developments.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
The main centers of cultural activity, including intellectual activity in particular, shifted from one period to another.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

These changes followed developments in Arab political life and the movement of political capitals. They also reflected the influence of the older intellectual traditions of the different lands brought into the Arab-Islamic empire.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
For this reason, the main centers of intellectual life in early Islam were different from those of the Abbasid period.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Further changes took place within the Abbasid period itself, continuing through the age of the regional dynasties, the Crusades, the Mongol invasions, and finally the period later described as the “age of decline.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

But during the early Islamic period, including the Umayyad age that still concerns us here, the main centers of intellectual activity were Mecca and Medina in the Hijaz; Basra and Kufa in Iraq; Damascus in Syria; and Fusṭāṭ, now Cairo, in Egypt.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
In Mecca and Medina, the main fields that flourished were jurisprudence, hadith, and history.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
This was because the Hijaz was the birthplace of Islam. From there, the new religion had spread through all the educational means available to it.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Mecca and Medina remained the main centers of the Prophet’s mission and of the Rightly Guided Caliphate, apart from the caliphate of ʿAlī, who made Kufa his center.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Basra and Kufa, by contrast, arose after the Arab conquest of Iraq during the caliphate of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Both quickly became major centers of the most advanced forms of cultural activity then available.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

In these two cities, the practical experience of people from the Hijaz combined with their knowledge of Islam, gained from having lived through its development from the beginning. Many of these people migrated to Kufa and Basra after the conquest.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
This was joined by the much older civilizational experience of the people of Iraq.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
They had inherited, or lived within, the cultural legacy of Babylon, Persia, and Assyria. The city of al-Ḥīra had also been influenced by these civilizations.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Some knowledge of Greek philosophy had reached Iraq through Christian monasteries in the north and through certain Persian schools.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
All these different forms of experience met in a region already marked by a rich cultural life and helped by rapid urban and economic development.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Before long, a sharp rivalry developed between Basra and Kufa.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
This rivalry became one of the forces encouraging intellectual growth in both cities.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

It eventually produced a division between a Basran school and a Kufan school. Each developed its own distinct approach to questions of jurisprudence, grammar, and literature, and later to questions of kalām as well.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Basra and Kufa remained among the most important centers of Arab thought for several generations, even after Baghdad had emerged as the unrivaled capital of Arab culture. We can see this in the deep and powerful effects they had on the development of Arab thought. They became starting points for some of the boldest and most independent schools of thought, such as the Muʿtazila, as well as for social movements with an intellectual basis, such as the Qarmaṭians and the Brethren of Purity.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

It seems to me that the conditions that placed Basra and Kufa in political opposition from the time the conflict between the Alids and the Umayyads became intense may have helped these schools of thought and social movements emerge in those two rebellious cities. Both cities also had large populations of mawālī, non-Arab clients and converts, who were among the strongest opponents of the Umayyads because the Umayyads stood for the idea of Arab supremacy.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Damascus, meanwhile, rose to great importance when it became the capital of the Umayyad caliphate. Scholars and writers came there from across the Arab state. Yet its cultural influence never reached the level of Basra or Kufa. Political conflict took up so much of the Umayyads’ attention that they devoted less effort to developing scholarship in their capital. Instead, they gave considerable attention to literature and writers, especially poets, whom they used to support their policies and attack their political opponents among the Anṣār, the Alids, and the Kharijites.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

This does not mean that Damascus had no intellectual life. Serious debates took place there over some of the questions raised by contact between Islam and Christianity. But these discussions remained within the limits of the official debate allowed in the Umayyad capital.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Take the problem of divine decree and the question of whether human beings are compelled to act or free to choose. Damascus could hardly have avoided discussing it when it had become the leading subject of intellectual debate in the schools of Iraq and the Hijaz. What mattered, however, was the position taken on the issue. In Damascus, the dominant position was the same as that of the Umayyad government: it supported the view that human beings do not have freedom of choice in their actions. We will later see how fiercely the Umayyad rulers fought the idea of free choice, and why.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

As for Fusṭāṭ, from the Arab conquest of Egypt in 20 AH/640 CE under ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb until the final years of Umayyad rule, it remained a center of learning dominated by the purely religious sciences, especially hadith and law. Its intellectual life therefore developed mainly through Islamic religious studies and the schools of law.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
C — Early Signs of Philosophical Thought
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Many later researchers, both Eastern and Western, have approached this question from only one side, although they disagree over which side matters.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Some explain the rise of philosophical thought around Islamic beliefs entirely through outside influences. The historian of philosophy T. J. de Boer is one of the clearest examples.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

First, he denies that the Qurʾan itself brought Muslims a body of doctrine. His argument is that the Qurʾan “gave Muslims a religion, not theories; they received rules, but they did not receive doctrines.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Second, he argues that once Muslims conquered other lands, “they found before them a fully developed Christian theology, as well as the doctrines of the followers of Zoroaster and the doctrines of the Brahmins.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

De Boer therefore has no doubt that the theological doctrines of the Muslim mutakallimūn were deeply influenced by Christian ideas. In his view, Islamic doctrine took shape under the influence of the Melkites and Jacobites in Damascus, and under the influence of Nestorian and Gnostic teachings in Basra.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

De Boer finally concludes that, alongside the considerations he has already described, there are “scattered indications that some of the earliest Muslims who defended free choice had Christian teachers. Purely philosophical elements then came first from the Gnostic schools, and later from translated books. These joined the Christian influences that had themselves been shaped by Greek philosophy in its final Eastern form.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Taken together, these views of De Boer—and they represent the position of many Western researchers—treat the philosophical discussion of Islamic beliefs among Arab Muslims as something that came entirely from outside.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

They give no real place to internal causes. Nor do they see any connection between the rise of philosophical thinking about Islamic beliefs and the actual conditions of Arab-Islamic life: not when these debates first appeared, not when they developed into the discipline known as kalām, and not when they later became fully philosophical questions with the emergence of Arab philosophy as something independent of kalām.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

It should be clear that views of this kind conflict, at least in one respect, not only with the facts of history but also with a sound scientific method of research. No sound method can accept that a particular kind of thinking simply appears in a society while remaining cut off from the internal conditions of that society at a particular stage of its development.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
What Engels wrote to Conrad Schmidt on 5 August 1890 applies to our subject to a large extent:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

“The whole of history must be studied anew, and the conditions of the different social formations must be examined in detail before any attempt is made to derive from them the political, legal, aesthetic, philosophical, and religious forms of thought that correspond to those conditions.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Another group of researchers on Arab-Islamic thought approaches the question in a way that comes closer to a sound method, but still does not examine social and political reality deeply enough to carry the logic of scientific inquiry through to its conclusion.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

This second group explains the rise of philosophical thought around Islamic beliefs through a very broad theory: that in its search for certainty, human thought passes through three stages—absolute belief, inner doubt, and finally rational conviction.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
When one representative of this view tries to apply this pattern to Arab-Islamic thought, however, he finds that he must qualify it:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

“Islamic thought was not primitive. Its acceptance in the first stage was therefore not naïve acceptance, but submission after resistance. Its doubt in the second stage was not hesitation over whether to believe, but uncertainty over whether the intended meaning had been fully understood. Most early Muslims therefore accepted the Qurʾanic verses according to their literal meaning. But some reflective minds began to doubt whether their first understanding had gone far enough. They returned to the text, considered its other possible meanings, and eventually settled on a view that gave them a form of rational certainty.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
This view, in one form or another, also appears in the work of other modern historians of Arab thought, especially Arab historians.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Its weakness is not only that it relies on broad generalizations. It also fails to begin from the ground of real social life and ask what actually drove this development.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Why did early Muslims move from accepting Qurʾanic verses in their literal sense, to doubting whether they had fully understood them, to rereading the text and considering other possible meanings, and finally to reaching a view that gave them a form of rational certainty?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Was this gradual change purely internal and reflective? Or was it connected to changes in the social and political life of Arab-Islamic society?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
If it was connected to those changes, how? Which events shaped its direction? And how closely were these changing intellectual positions connected to changes in the society itself?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Those who take this view give us no answer to any of these questions. Their explanation therefore remains, on one side, broad and abstract and, on the other, idealist in the way it approaches the subject.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

If we compare these first two positions with that of a third group of major modern researchers, such as Muṣṭafā ʿAbd al-Rāziq and Aḥmad Amīn, we find an approach much closer to a scientific method because it avoids looking at the problem from only one side.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Muṣṭafā ʿAbd al-Rāziq, for example, writes about matters of belief under the Rightly Guided Caliphs:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

“Questions of belief under the Rightly Guided Caliphs remained much as they had been in the time of the Prophet. But the Prophet proclaimed the word of revelation, and no believer could turn away from it. Any disagreement among Muslims was settled by referring it back to the Messenger of God.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

“Under the Rightly Guided Caliphs, disagreements did arise over questions that required independent judgment. Although these questions were connected to practical rulings, they became important enough to form the basis of lasting divisions among Muslims. Their importance grew until they became connected to questions of belief, and many Islamic sects were built on their foundations.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

ʿAbd al-Rāziq then traces these disputes in concrete historical terms, beginning with the disagreement over the caliphate after the Prophet’s death, moving through the events that followed, and then through the rise of different schools and factions. He finally concludes:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
“Although the arguments between these schools were based mainly on transmitted religious texts, they were also mixed with rational inquiry.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

This account places the rise of “rational inquiry” within real historical conditions. Its starting point was the first dispute over the caliphate. That dispute then developed until it produced schools that were political in content but religious in form. Debate between those schools created an intellectual basis from which rational inquiry—or what we have called philosophical thought—could begin.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

We agree with this concrete account of the conditions in which this kind of thinking emerged. But, as we have repeatedly stressed, this does not mean ignoring outside influences, especially cultural ones. Those influences helped philosophical thought move beyond its first simple beginnings and develop into more complex and mature forms. In other words, they helped move it from the concrete level of social and political reality to the level of theoretical awareness.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Aḥmad Amīn also traces the beginnings of these debates—which later took on a rational and theoretical form in kalām—back to their first political roots in Arab-Islamic life. At the same time, he does not ignore the part played by outside influences in helping these debates develop into the more systematic theoretical form they reached under the Abbasids.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

It is true that Aḥmad Amīn also uses the same broad theory we saw in the second group of researchers. He expresses it by saying that every religious belief begins as a simple but powerful faith. At first, it pays little attention to disagreement or investigation. It accepts the foundations of religion and believes in them fully, without much desire for analysis or philosophy.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Then comes the stage of investigation and reflection. Religious questions begin to take on a scholarly and philosophical character, and religious thinkers turn to philosophy to strengthen their arguments and support their proofs.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

“This happened in Judaism, this happened in Christianity, and this happened in Islam. The first Islamic age nearly passed in a state of faith with little argument. Then, once people had settled down, they began to examine and investigate. They widened the scope of their inquiry, compared similar cases, distinguished differences and points of agreement, and this necessarily led to different ways of looking at things, and therefore to differences of opinion and doctrine.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

It is true that Aḥmad Amīn uses this general theory in an idealist form. But he does not leave it floating in abstraction or push it further into idealism. He connects it to real historical factors. Whether he intended this or not, that connection helps strip away its idealist shell.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
This becomes clear when he discusses internal causes, including political ones. Speaking of those political causes, he writes:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

“Sometimes a teaching belonging to one of the different sects is described as though it were purely religious doctrine, a question of belief and nothing more. But if we examine its origin carefully, we find that it was political. Take the question of the Muslim who commits a major sin: is he an unbeliever or a believer? It seems that this was not originally a purely theological debate. Its source was the judgment that the political parties passed on one another…”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
He goes on to say that political disagreement became “a major cause of religious disagreement, and a cause of doctrines and sects.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
After describing the political conflict in detail and identifying the different sides—the Shīʿa, the Umayyads, the Kharijites, and the neutral party, the Murjiʾa—he reaches this conclusion:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

“This political conflict, which took on a religious form, also contributed to disagreements over the meaning of faith and unbelief, major and minor sins, the status of the person who commits a major sin, and similar questions. They were then drawn into disagreements over secondary matters as well, until each group gradually became a separate sect with its own disagreements over both fundamental and secondary questions.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

This way of analyzing the problem closely agrees with the analysis we adopted in an earlier chapter. In our view, it identifies the indirect political and social roots from which philosophical thinking about Islamic beliefs emerged.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
What remains is to trace the historical course through which this kind of thinking began to develop.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

We do not say that we must identify its “direct causes.” Intellectual developments, like historical stages in the development of society, cannot be assigned simple direct causes. There are no sharp boundaries separating one stage from another. Two stages may coexist for a long time, and intellectual developments are even more complicated in this respect.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

So if we want to identify the historical course of this development, or the point at which that course began to take shape, we have to look at particular historical events and ask how they affected the general climate of thought during this period rather than another.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

We must also look at what was distinctive about those events, at the kind of effect they had on the dominant intellectual questions of the time, at the internal forces working beneath the surface, and at the way those internal forces interacted with influences coming from outside.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Second: The Problem of Divine Decree
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
The problem of divine decree was one of the first major questions through which Arab thought began moving toward the kind of rational inquiry that prepared the way for philosophical thought.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

We have a great deal of historical evidence showing that discussion of divine decree and predestination among Arab and Muslim thinkers had already become an intellectual debate about the responsibility of the individual for his own actions around the middle of the first Islamic century—that is, around the middle of the seventh century CE.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

“In the later days of the Companions, disagreement appeared with the Qadarites. They discussed divine decree and human power—the ability of a person to act through his own power—as did Maʿbad al-Juhanī, Ghaylān al-Dimashqī, and Jaʿd ibn Dirham. The Companions who were still alive rejected their views: ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās, Jābir, Anas, Abū Hurayra, ʿUqba ibn ʿĀmir, and others of their generation. They advised those who came after them not to greet these men, not to visit them if they became ill, and not to pray over them when they died.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

If we add to this what we know about the deaths of these Companions—Jābir died in 50 AH/670 CE, while Anas, the last of them, died in 93 AH/712 CE—we can reasonably conclude that the issue was already being widely discussed in intellectual and religious circles before the 50s AH, that is, before the 670s CE.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
This conclusion is supported by Ṭāshkubrīzāda, who says that:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

“The disagreement”—meaning the disagreement over divine decree—“developed gradually until the final days of the Companions. Then Maʿbad al-Juhanī, Ghaylān al-Dimashqī, Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ, ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd, and Yūnus al-Aswārī appeared. They disagreed over divine decree and over attributing all things to God’s determination, and so on, until the principles of Muʿtazilism emerged.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
This passage suggests that the issue was already being discussed even before Maʿbad and Ghaylān, whom some researchers describe as the first people to speak about divine decree.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

The view that comes closest to the historical evidence, then, is that the question had already been raised before either man appeared. Ṭāshkubrīzāda’s wording itself points in that direction: “The disagreement developed gradually until the final days of the Companions, then Maʿbad appeared…”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
This not only fits the historical evidence. It also fits the way history itself develops.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Intellectual movements do not normally begin at a sharp and precisely identifiable point. We cannot usually say that a particular intellectual development was created by one person, or by a few people, at one exact moment.
